ambiguous.item: Ransomware encrypts the file server
ambiguous.why: Encryption without consent both denies access (availability) and alters the stored data, and modern double-extortion ransomware also breaches confidentiality, so the 'primary' impact is a house convention rather than pure doctrine.

ambiguous.item: Firmware replaced with a tampered build
ambiguous.why: The unauthorised modification is the integrity event, but a tampered firmware build is normally installed precisely to harvest or leak data, which a practitioner could argue is the real loss.

ambiguous.item: Offline immutable backups
ambiguous.why: Backups restore service (availability), but 'immutable' is an integrity property and a strict reading of 'primarily protects availability' could push this toward integrity.

ambiguous.item: Role-based access control
ambiguous.why: RBAC is doctrinally a confidentiality/integrity control, yet in the stated ransomware scenario least-privilege is exactly what limits blast radius and keeps records reachable, which is an availability argument.

ambiguous.item: Tested restore procedure
ambiguous.why: It is an administrative/process control rather than a technical safeguard, so a marker looking only for controls that directly sustain uptime could exclude it.

ambiguous.item: Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
ambiguous.why: Strict non-repudiation normally requires cryptographic signing by the actor; an audit log is often taught as accountability or integrity evidence rather than true non-repudiation.

ambiguous.item: A code generated by an authenticator app on your phone
ambiguous.why: Doctrine treats the possessed device as the factor, but the artefact actually typed in is a value the user reads and knows, and some texts label transmitted OTPs as a knowledge-adjacent factor.

ambiguous.item: A locked door on the server room
ambiguous.why: A plain keyed lock is unambiguously physical, but if the lock is an electronic badge or cipher reader (the common modern case) the access-decision logic is a technical control with a physical enclosure.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties is a managerial/administrative principle, but on payment approvals it is normally enforced by workflow configuration in the finance system, which is a technical control.

ambiguous.item: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
ambiguous.why: It is physical in ISC2 terms, though the badge back-end is technical and the turnstile only works because of an administrative access-authorisation process, so a practitioner could class the whole safeguard differently.

ambiguous.item: A peer offers to sell you leaked ISC2 exam questions, and you decline and report it
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Exam-integrity cases are conventionally filed under Canon IV, but refusing to participate in theft of copyrighted material is squarely honest/legal conduct under Canon II.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: The refusal is an honesty act (II), but it happens inside a client engagement and Canon III's duty to serve principals honestly could equally be cited; a false audit report also endangers public trust (Canon I).

ambiguous.item: You correct a status report you had already sent, once you realise it overstated your progress
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: Self-correction is honesty (II), yet accurate reporting to the principal who commissioned the work is exactly what Canon III's diligent service means, so the split depends on whether you weight the virtue or the relationship.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client their deadline is too short for a competent test rather than rushing it
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Refusing to deliver substandard work is Canon III competence, but telling an uncomfortable truth to a paying client is also plain honesty under Canon II.

ambiguous.item: You disclose to a client that a specialised cloud engagement is outside your current competence
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: 'Render only services for which you are competent' is verbatim Canon III, but the act described is a disclosure, i.e. honesty, which reads as Canon II.

ambiguous.item: A vendor ignores your reports of a medical-device firmware flaw while patients remain at risk, and you keep pressing for a fix
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
ambiguous.defensible_alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: Patient safety makes this Canon I, but persistent responsible disclosure against vendor resistance is also the professional-conduct behaviour Canon IV is meant to model and protect.

ambiguous.item: Discontinue the legacy file-sharing service entirely
ambiguous.why: Removing the activity outright is textbook avoidance, but retiring a vulnerable component is also commonly written up as a mitigating/remediation action in a risk register.

ambiguous.item: Document the remaining chance of a laptop stolen while unlocked, and have the head of IT sign it off
ambiguous.why: Formal sign-off of residual risk is acceptance, though the item sits downstream of encryption controls and a reader could treat the whole encryption-plus-residual package as mitigation.

ambiguous.item: Access to company systems is granted on the principle of least privilege
ambiguous.why: It is a broad mandatory intent statement (policy), but it names a specific enforceable rule applied uniformly across systems, which is how a standard reads.

ambiguous.item: All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image
ambiguous.why: Mandatory uniform technical requirement, i.e. a standard/baseline, though 'approved hardened image' without a named specification could be read as a policy statement pointing at a separate standard.
